source_text: Dicis trahi naturae conditione peccatum, qui vis hoc malum a voluntate primi hominis accidisse. Differo hic responsionem, qua convincendus es quod sine verecundia mentiaris. Sed quod ad praesentem locum spectat, colligo, et sapientiae ratiocinanti credo, quod naturam videlicet diabolicam sine ambiguitate definias. Nam si in ea vel per eam est, propter quod homo a diabolo possidetur; irrefutabiliter diaboli est, per quod Dei imaginem sibi potuit vindicare. Immo nec imago Dei est, quae per exortum suum in regno diaboli est.
pass_a_gloss: You say that sin is drawn by the condition of nature, you who want this evil to have happened from the will of the first human. I defer here the answer by which you are to be convicted that you lie without shame. But what looks to the present place, I gather, and I believe wisdom reasoning, that you define a diabolical nature without ambiguity. For if in it or through it there is that on account of which a human is possessed by the devil; irrefutably the devil's is that through which he could claim the image of God for himself. Nay it is not even the image of God, which through its own coming-forth is in the kingdom of the devil.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: You say that sin is inherited through the condition of nature, while claiming that this evil arose from the first human being's will. I postpone here the reply that will convict you of shameless lying. For the present issue, however, I draw this conclusion, trusting reasoned understanding: you unambiguously define nature as diabolical. For if that through which a human being is possessed by the devil exists in nature or comes through nature, then that by which the devil could claim God's image for himself indisputably belongs to the devil (compare Genesis 1:26–27). Indeed, something that is in the devil's kingdom by its very birth is not even God's image (Genesis 1:26–27).

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
